request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]          Admission Date: [REDACTED]      Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

History of Present Illness:
A 79-year-old male with a history of prostate cancer presented with progressively worsening double vision and eventual right eye ptosis. Neurological examination revealed complete third and sixth nerve palsies on the right side. MR imaging showed an enhancing soft tissue mass involving the clivus, pituitary fossa, cavernous sinus, and posterior nasal cavity. An endonasal transsphenoidal approach to the sphenoid sinus was carried out to obtain a biopsy of the lesion. A histopathological diagnosis of metastatic melanoma was made, and evaluation was undertaken by the oncology team.

Hospital Course Summary:
During the patient's hospital stay, he underwent a number of diagnostic tests and a biopsy following which he was diagnosed with metastatic melanoma. The medical team consulted with the oncology team, who evaluated the patient and recommended further treatment options. The patient's clinical condition stabilised, and he was discharged with the oncology team's recommended course of treatment.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient's medical condition at discharge was stable, with no further significant neurological or ophthalmological deficits.

Discharge Medications:
No medications were prescribed at the time of discharge.

Follow-up Care:
The oncology team recommended further outpatient treatment and follow-up evaluations for the patient, which the patient accepted.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was advised to follow up with the oncology team on a regular basis, and to report any new or concerning symptoms.
Discharge Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Discharge Condition:
Stable.

Discharge Plan:
The patient was discharged with the recommended course of treatment and follow-up evaluations by the oncology team.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The principal diagnosis is secondary malignant neoplasm of bone, category C79.

1. **Chapter letter: C.** The condition chiefly responsible for this admission was metastatic melanoma, confirmed on biopsy. It explains the third and sixth nerve palsies and the ptosis. Those are presenting signs, so they are not the principal diagnosis. The biopsy is a procedure, and the history of prostate cancer is a comorbidity, so neither of those is principal either. The cancer is malignant, so the chapter is C.

2. **Digits: 79.** The patient was admitted to investigate a metastatic lesion, so the secondary neoplasm is the principal diagnosis rather than the primary melanoma. The primary site is not stated. The mass is centred on the clivus, which is skull-base bone. Secondary malignant neoplasm of bone falls under category C79 (C79.5 at the fourth character).

The mass also extends into the pituitary fossa, cavernous sinus, sphenoid sinus and nasal cavity. If the coder judged one of those sites to be dominant, the category could instead be C79 (other specified sites) or C78 (respiratory organs, which includes the sinuses). I chose bone because the clivus appears to be the centre of the lesion.

CODE: C79
